newsitem.title: GERMANY: Most German executives see prompt EMU start - poll.
newsitem.headline: Most German executives see prompt EMU start - poll.

text.p: Over four-fifths of German executives expect the launch of Europe's single currency to go ahead as planned on January 1, 1999, a survey of top managers at over 100 firms showed on Thursday.

The survey, to be published on Friday by Manager magazine, also found that many companies planned to switch over to using euros as a means of payment before the currency is issued in notes and coins in 2002.

Over half the survey sample had a positive attitude towards the European currency reform -- in stark contrast to the German public, where polls regularly show that about three-quarters of people are against giving up the stable mark.
Only 13 percent of those asked by the Gemini Consulting polling organisation said they expected currency union to have negative consequences, according to Manager.
The study also revealed that businesses were still very unprepared for the euro, with companies tending to treat the new currency as a technical rather than a strategic problem.

Doubts have mounted recently in Germany over whether Bonn will be able to meet key fiscal criteria in the Maastricht treaty on government union. Economic performance in 1997 will be judged by European leaders in a year's time to decide on which countries are fit to join the euro.

Economists and some central bankers have urged a delay until Germany manages to get state finances under control, but the government is adamant it will be able to cut borrowing and lead Europe into a stability-based monetary union.
